# Soonhwan Kwon

## PhD Candidate in Political Science

**Indiana University Bloomington**

I study the political economy of **housing**, **welfare regimes**, and **wealth inequality**, with particular attention to how housing policies and institutions shape redistributive politics and political behavior. I use longitudinal survey data, quasi-experimental designs, and survey experiments to study these questions comparatively across advanced democracies.

## Current research

::: {.research-grid}
::: {.research-card}
### Toward Homeownership

My job-market paper examines whether the 2023 deregulation of mortgage finance and housing transactions in Seoul changed renters' prospects of upward mobility before they became homeowners.

[Seoul study →](research.qmd#toward-homeownership)
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Into Homeownership

My Netherlands study asks how public protection against mortgage risk changes financial expectations and support for redistribution after renters become homeowners.

[Netherlands study →](research.qmd#into-homeownership)
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Outside Homeownership

My New York City study examines how different forms of renter protection shape beliefs about unequal opportunity, meritocracy, and the fairness of the economic system.

[New York study →](research.qmd#outside-homeownership)
:::
:::

## Research agenda

Why do homeownership-centered institutions remain politically durable even as homeownership becomes harder to attain? I argue that housing policy helps reproduce or challenge this order by shaping how citizens approach homeownership, experience its risks after purchase, or seek security while remaining renters. These policy-shaped pathways can, in turn, reshape political interests and solidarity around redistribution.

My dissertation traces policy feedback across three points in the housing trajectory: **toward homeownership, into homeownership, and outside homeownership**. Related projects extend this agenda to wealth inequality, debt-financed homeownership, and the conditions under which renter-support policies become either an alternative to ownership or a stepping stone toward it.
